summary: For 6-7 year-olds, using structure shifts from noticing a pattern to deliberately exploiting it: reordering 3+9 as 9+3 to count on from the larger addend, using place value so 47+10 changes only the tens digit, and seeing a square as a special rectangle because both have four sides and four right angles. The core teaching move is to make the efficient and inefficient approaches visible side by side so the child feels why structure pays off — fewer counts, a digit that predictably changes, a shared property — rather than being told a rule, and then justifies why the shortcut is allowed.
misconceptions: Always counts on from the first number written, not the larger, because order is treated as fixed
Adds 10 by counting in ones or by changing the ones digit (47+10 = 48) rather than seeing the tens digit change
Believes a square is not a rectangle because they look different / have different names (prototype and mutually-exclusive categories)
Applies commutativity to subtraction (34-10 handled like 10-34)

activities.title: Choose your start: count on from the larger addend
steps: For 3 + 9, first count on starting from 3 — draw or hop all nine moves across a number line and watch it crawl from 3 to 12.
Now start from 9 instead and count on three — land on 12 in just three hops.
Say what is the same (both reach 12) and what is different (far fewer hops when you start from the larger number).
Answer: why is swapping the order allowed here? Connect to 'the order you add in doesn't change the total.'
Try the same choice for 2 + 8 and 8 + 2: decide which number to start from and explain your choice before you count.
activities.insight: Starting the count-on from the larger addend reaches the same total with far less work, and this is allowed because addition can be done in any order (commutativity).

activities.title: Adding ten: predict which digit moves
steps: Before adding, predict: when I add 10 to 47, which digit will change and which will stay the same?
Add one ten-rod to a base-ten representation of 47, or move the tens on a place-value / arrow-card setup, and check: the tens change (4→5) and the ones stay the same, giving 57.
Repeat the predict-then-check for 63 + 10, saying which digit changes and why before you do it.
Explain in your own words why adding ten leaves the ones digit alone.
activities.insight: For two-digit numbers that do not cross into the hundreds, adding ten changes only the tens digit (it goes up by one) because ten is one whole ten; place value, not counting in ones, tells you which column moves.

activities.title: Is a square a kind of rectangle?
steps: Sort a mixed set of shapes into groups by property: all shapes with four sides, and all shapes with four right angles.

Overlap the two groups (e.g. two overlapping hoops): the overlap holds every shape with four sides and four right angles, which is the rectangle set. See that squares land there alongside the other rectangles, because they have both properties.
Answer: what is the same about a square and a rectangle, and what is different?
State why a square counts as a special rectangle, pointing to the shared properties rather than the name or how it looks.
activities.insight: A square is a special rectangle because it has the defining properties of a rectangle (four sides, four right angles); classification should be based on properties, not names or appearance.

activities.title: Does the shortcut still work? Bounding the structure
steps: Discuss the diagnostic situation: To work out 3 + 9, Sam started at 3 and counted on nine more; Maya started at 9 and counted on three more. Both got 12. Is one way better, and why?
Say why Maya's way is better (fewer to count on) AND why swapping is allowed (order of adding doesn't change the total).
Test whether the swap idea has limits: does swapping the order also work for 12 take away 4 — could I do 4 take away 12 instead? Explain why not.
Give the general rule you've found: reordering is safe for addition but not for subtraction.
activities.insight: The reorder-to-the-larger strategy depends on commutativity, which holds for addition but not subtraction; a learner who understands the structure can say where it applies and where it breaks.

checkQuestion: To work out 3 + 9, Sam started at 3 and counted on nine more. Maya started at 9 and counted on three more. They both got 12. Is one way better than the other? Why?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child preferring Maya's way because starting from the larger number means fewer to count on, AND justifying that swapping is allowed because the order of adding doesn't change the total.
